entries.clue: Traitor getting fed up with East End bully (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' turns the word to read bottom to top
Cockneys from London's East End famously drop their Hs

blocks.note: HECTOR (to bully) said without its H

annotation.surface: A turncoat, sick of being pushed around by a London thug, finally switches sides.
annotation.walkthrough: The East End is London's Cockney heartland, where an initial H goes unspoken, so HECTOR becomes 'ECTOR.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who crosses over to the enemy side betrays their own, so is a traitor to it.

entries.clue: Going through vapid lyrics without enthusiasm (4)

indicators.note: the answer passes through the middle of the next words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the last two letters of vapid and the first two of lyrics

annotation.surface: Someone sings dull song lyrics with no feeling at all.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the space between the two words, which is why it is easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: An adverb for a lazy, half-hearted manner: doing a job this way is doing it with no enthusiasm.

entries.clue: Rising repercussion of crime (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters read upward

blocks.note: split as RE (about) + PERCUSSION, where a drum is a percussion instrument

annotation.surface: The consequences of a crime come back to haunt the criminal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Repercussion' has to be split into RE + PERCUSSION. REDRUM, read upward, is also the famous mirror-writing in the film The Shining.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the killing of a person is the gravest crime there is.

entries.clue: It’s about a leaning in characters, primarily (7)

definitions.text: It’s about a leaning in characters, primarily

indicators.note: IT'S goes round the other letters, as 'about' means around
primarily means first of all, so take the first letter of each of the words before it

blocks.note: taken as written, split around the middle
first letters of A, Leaning, In, Characters

annotation.surface: A definition: sloping type is simply lettering that leans.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition, since a leaning is chiefly what marks out this typeface.
annotation.definitionFit: The &lit reads straight: this is the typeface whose characters slant, so a leaning in them is its defining feature.

entries.clue: Tarzan? He abandoned noted childhood home (8)

indicators.note: abandoned also means wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose

annotation.surface: Tarzan, raised by apes, left behind the jungle where he grew up.
annotation.walkthrough: Tarzan's jungle upbringing points to the wrong childhood; the famous one is Jesus's.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Jesus grew up in this Galilean town, making it the best-known childhood home of all.

entries.clue: Disadvantages seen with crime plot (10)

annotation.surface: A plan to commit a crime has its downsides.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crime plot' reads as one phrase; 'plot' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a secret plan agreed between plotters to do harm.

entries.clue: Group of flyers finding something funny with broken leg (6)

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so the letters of LEG are broken up and reassembled

annotation.surface: Someone laughs at a man with a broken leg, which is hardly a joke.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flyers' suggests airline passengers; the group is of geese.
annotation.definitionFit: The collective noun for geese, birds that fly, though strictly only when they are on the ground.

entries.clue: Strike top and bottom (8)

blocks.note: the top of anything, as in the head of a table

annotation.surface: A brawler lands a blow top to bottom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top and bottom' reads as 'from head to foot'; it is two body parts laid end to end.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb for a particular strike: ramming someone with your forehead.

entries.clue: Bouquet in Rome, as they say there (5)

indicators.note: put the words into the language spoken in Rome, Italian

blocks.note: the Italian preposition for 'in' before a city

annotation.surface: A visitor admires the scent of flowers in Rome, using the local phrase.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay asks for Italian: 'in Rome' as a Roman would say it.
annotation.definitionFit: Bouquet is the wine-taster's word for the smell of a wine, so a smell or scent.

entries.clue: Gathering for a drink by the sound of it (4)

indicators.note: we want a word that sounds like another

blocks.note: British slang for an alcoholic drink, short for beverage

annotation.surface: An invitation to meet up for a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: A bevvy is British slang for a drink, usually beer; the answer is spelt with one V.
annotation.definitionFit: A collective noun for a group, originally of quails or of women, now any gathering.

entries.clue: $500 loan girl’s arranged (6,4)

indicators.note: the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500

annotation.surface: Someone has fixed up a five-hundred-dollar loan for a young woman.
annotation.walkthrough: '$500' reads as one sum of money; the $ is the definition and the 500 is the Roman D.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is the symbol itself: $ is the mark written before an amount in US currency.

entries.clue: New edition of Proust causing bewilderment (6)

indicators.note: a new edition reworks the text, so the letters are reworked

annotation.surface: A fresh edition of Proust's vast novel leaves its readers baffled.
annotation.walkthrough: Proust is the French novelist whose seven-volume 'In Search of Lost Time' could well leave a reader dazed.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a dazed state in which you cannot think clearly, as bewildered people are.

entries.clue: Horse rider and bike rider’s location: touring the East of Germany (10)

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go round it, so PILLION goes round OST

blocks.note: the passenger seat on a motorbike

annotation.surface: A cyclist and a horseman set off together on a tour of eastern Germany.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The East of Germany' reads as a region; it asks for the German word for east.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: the rider mounted on one of the leading horses drawing a carriage.

entries.clue: So-called Philistine (another name of mine) likes a little smut? Cut minister, cut! (8)

definitions.text: So-called Philistine (another name of mine) likes a little smut? Cut minister, cut!

indicators.note: a cut minister is one cut short, losing his last letter

blocks.note: to chop, as with an axe

annotation.surface: A four-line comic verse about the setter Philistine and his taste for a little smut.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is itself an example of the answer: two rhyming couplets of comic verse opening with a person's name, Philistine, rhyming with 'mine' and 'minister'.
annotation.definitionFit: The &lit works because the whole clue is a short comic biographical verse, the form invented by Edmund Clerihew Bentley.

entries.clue: Radical start of divisive racist movement (7)

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
the letters of RACIST move about

annotation.surface: A political party with an extreme, divisive, racist platform.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Racist movement' reads as a political group; the movement is the letters shifting.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: extreme, far-reaching measures, as in radical or sweeping change.

entries.clue: Upset as an agricultural worker may be (2,1,5)

definitions.text: as an agricultural worker may be

blocks.clueFragment: as an agricultural worker may be
blocks.note: standing in a flooded rice field

annotation.surface: A farm labourer is having a bad day.
annotation.walkthrough: In British slang a paddy is a fit of temper; a paddy is also a flooded rice field, where a farmhand may well stand.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: in British English, someone in a temper tantrum is upset; literally, a rice farmer works in the field.

entries.clue: Weapon kept by those people (3,4)

indicators.note: what is kept by someone is held inside, so THEY hold ARM

blocks.note: as in firearm, the arms trade

annotation.surface: A description of an armed force: a weapon held by a group of people.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition, since a nation's soldiers are exactly the people who keep its weapons.
annotation.definitionFit: The &lit reads straight: a land force is a body of people entrusted with weapons.

entries.clue: Trouble for spy boss? (8)

blocks.note: MI's: of Military Intelligence, the British spy agencies MI5 and MI6

annotation.surface: The head of the secret service is in trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spy boss' reads as one phrase; it has to become a possessive, the head belonging to British Military Intelligence.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: harm or trouble, often playful, as in children getting into it.

entries.clue: Booklet and what follows (7)

blocks.note: split into two words, BOOK and LET, each starting a definition
as in booking a table or a seat
in tennis, after a let the point is replayed with a fresh serve

annotation.surface: A pamphlet and its follow-up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Booklet' must be split into BOOK and LET. A let is a tennis serve that clips the net and is replayed, so what follows is a second go at serving, read as RE-SERVE.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: booking a table secures it in advance, and after a tennis let the server has to serve again.

entries.clue: Personal hint (8)

annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are also pronounced differently: the adjective ends like 'mutt', the verb like 'mate'.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: private or personal matters, and to suggest something without saying it outright.

entries.clue: Mounting desire to steal underwear in this neighbourhood (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounting means climbing, so the letters read upward
a thief takes the goods into himself, so YEN takes BRA inside it

annotation.surface: A local thief with a growing urge to steal lingerie from washing lines.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mounting desire' reads as a growing urge; 'mounting' is the upward instruction for the whole assembly, done after the stealing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: close at hand, in the surrounding area.

entries.clue: In bed, agreed to be most reserved (6)

indicators.note: the word for 'agreed' is put in the word for 'bed'

annotation.surface: A couple in bed settle on who is the shyest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In bed, agreed' reads as a pillow-talk conversation, but the comma hides a container instruction reading 'agreed in bed'.
annotation.definitionFit: A superlative synonym: shyest, most bashful, the most reserved of all.

entries.clue: Alluding to glimpse when caught (6)

indicators.note: caught by the ear, i.e. heard

annotation.surface: Someone mentions a brief glimpse of a fugitive at the moment of capture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' suggests an arrest; it means heard, so the glimpse is to be spoken.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: quoting or mentioning something as an example is referring or alluding to it.

entries.clue: Standard message returned to nearest vacant house (10)

indicators.note: the letters of EMAIL come back the other way
emptied of its middle, leaving only the outside letters

blocks.note: the standard score, as in golf

annotation.surface: A standard letter is sent back to the closest empty home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vacant house' reads as an empty home; 'vacant' belongs to 'nearest', and 'house' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A legislative chamber is a house, as in the House of Commons or House of Lords.

entries.clue: Ask cop why not get naked in this part of London (4)

indicators.note: stripping each word removes its outer letters

blocks.note: the middle letter of each of the four words

annotation.surface: A cheeky challenge to a policeman: why not strip off in a racy London district?
annotation.walkthrough: The surface fits because the district is famous for nightlife and, historically, strip clubs.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a district of London's West End, and 'this' points back to the surface's striptease.

entries.clue: Therefore very mediocre (2-2)

blocks.note: as in 'it rained, so we stayed in'

annotation.surface: A verdict that something is extremely mediocre.
annotation.walkthrough: Two different senses of the same little word, one after the other.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: neither good nor bad, just middling.

entries.clue: Mope having prepared tea, say? (5)

indicators.note: as you say it, i.e. by sound

blocks.note: what is done to tea in the pot

annotation.surface: Someone sulks after putting the kettle on.
annotation.walkthrough: The homophone is of the past tense: tea that has been prepared has been brewed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to dwell gloomily on your troubles.

entries.clue: I got rid of vehicle first and disappeared (8)

indicators.note: the vehicle is placed first, ahead of the words that precede it in the clue

blocks.note: past tense: cast off, as a snake its skin

annotation.surface: A criminal dumps the getaway van and goes to ground.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is in reverse order; 'first' tells you to move the vehicle to the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: went out of sight completely.
